terms.grammar: noun phrase: fīlia with the genitive rēgis
terms.comment: As with prince, Latin says it with a phrase. Morgan–Owens adds prīncipissa, a medieval word, for a woman who rules a principality or a prince’s wife.

terms.gloss: a king’s daughter (in the poets); usually a queen
terms.comment: Of Ariadne and Medea in the poets, and of the daughters of Darius in Curtius (Lewis & Short); but a listener hears “queen” first (see queen).

terms.grammar: noun phrase: virgo with the adjective rēgia

phrases.latin: hīs duōbus, ut ante dictum est, duae Tulliae rēgis fīliae nūpserant, et ipsae longē disparēs mōribus
phrases.english: these two, as I said before, had married the two Tullias, the king’s daughters, who were themselves very different in character

sources: Lewis & Short: rex · Lewis & Short: filia · Lewis & Short: regina · Lewis & Short: regius · Lewis & Short: virgo
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. princess.
